steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper proposing Prompt Highlighter, an inference-time method that lets users highlight parts of the input to steer multi-modal LLM generation. Motivate it against prompt engineering, explain the mechanism briefly, mention benchmark results, and list contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- LLMs, VLMs and prompt engineering as the usual way of control; its limits
- Our idea: Prompt Highlighter, token-level highlighting
- How it works: classifier-free guidance + attention activation
- Compatibility with multi-modal LLMs
- Benchmark results
- Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Background
  - LLMs: big progress on many NLP tasks
  - extended to vision-language tasks via visual-language alignment and instruction tuning -> VLMs
  - autoregressive, generation conditioned on input context
  - prompt engineering = common interaction; diverse formats/content to steer output
  - relies on empirical intuition, careful context design, hard for non-experts
  - even carefully crafted prompts (concept of 'compactness') can give unpredictable outputs (left part of figure)
- Prompt Highlighter
  - instead of prompt-level manipulation: token-level user interaction, personalized generation
  - like a highlighter tool in a text editor: emphasize desired parts
- Mechanism
  - regular + unconditional input context pair, different textual embeddings in highlighted tokens
  - classifier-free guidance on predicted token probabilities
  - probing cross-token attention maps: attention scores correlate with semantic significance of tokens
  - attention activation: adjusted attention mask reweights scores for highlighted part
- Compatibility
  - vs vanilla inference: more controllable, closer to user needs
  - works with transformer-based multi-modal LLMs: patch-wise visual token mapping (LLaVA) and query-based (Q-Former)
  - goes beyond prompt engineering
- Results
  - comprehensive multi-modal benchmarks
  - highlighting full image context improves image captions and QA
  - mitigates hallucination by focusing on reliable context
  - no extra training; improves LLaVA-v1.5; 2nd place on MMBench and MME-perception leaderboards
- Contributions
  - (1) fine-grained human-model interaction, plug-and-play, token-level, controllable
  - (2) extensive experiments, significant improvement

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Large Language Models (LLMs) have made a lot of progress on many natural language processing tasks. These models were then extended to handle vision-language tasks using visual-language alignment and instruction tuning, which gave more advances. This led to Vision Language Models (VLMs), which can generate text from multi-modal inputs. Because they are autoregressive, the usual generation process in LLMs and VLMs (multi-modal LLMs) is mainly conditioned on the input context. Prompt engineering has become a common way for humans to interact with language models, where people use different formats and content of prompts to push the generation toward the outcome they want. But prompt engineering often relies on empirical intuition and needs careful design of the context, so it is less accessible for non-experts. As the left part of the figure shows, even very carefully crafted prompts that clearly convey the concept of ‘compactness’ can give unpredictable outputs that don't meet the requirements.

We propose a new inference approach, Prompt Highlighter, which enables token-level user interactions for personalized generations, instead of manipulating contexts at the prompt level (i.e., prompt engineering) to control the generation of LMs. With our method users can interact with multi-modal LLMs in a way that is like using a highlighter tool on the input context in a text editor, so they can emphasize the parts they want by highlighting them.

To get this highlighting mechanism, we build a regular and unconditional input context pair with different textual embeddings in the highlighted tokens. Then we can adjust how much the model focuses on the highlighted components using classifier-free guidance on predicted token probabilities. Also, by probing cross-token attention maps, we found a robust correlation between attention scores and the semantic significance of tokens. This suggests that in the autoregressive generation process of language models, the semantic relationship between tokens can be represented to some extent by their attention scores. Based on this, we introduce an attention activation strategy that adjusts the attention weights for a highlighted part. Prompt Highlighter uses an adjusted attention mask to reweight the corresponding attention scores, so the generation focuses more on the highlighted parts.

- Compatibility
  - vs vanilla inference: more controllable, closer to user needs
  - works with patch-wise (LLaVA) and query-based (Q-Former) visual token mapping
  - beyond prompt engineering
- Results
  - highlighting full image improves captions and QA, mitigates hallucination
  - no extra training, improves LLaVA-v1.5, 2nd place on MMBench and MME-perception
- Contributions: (1) token-level plug-and-play interaction; (2) extensive experiments

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Large Language Models (LLMs) have made a lot of progress on many natural language processing tasks. These models were then extended to handle vision-language tasks using visual-language alignment and instruction tuning, which gave more advances. This led to Vision Language Models (VLMs), which can generate text from multi-modal inputs. Because they are autoregressive, the usual generation process in LLMs and VLMs (multi-modal LLMs) is mainly conditioned on the input context. Prompt engineering has become a common way for humans to interact with language models, where people use different formats and content of prompts to push the generation toward the outcome they want. But prompt engineering often relies on empirical intuition and needs careful design of the context, so it is less accessible for non-experts. As the left part of the figure shows, even very carefully crafted prompts that clearly convey the concept of ‘compactness’ can give unpredictable outputs that don't meet the requirements.

We propose a new inference approach, Prompt Highlighter, which enables token-level user interactions for personalized generations, instead of manipulating contexts at the prompt level (i.e., prompt engineering) to control the generation of LMs. With our method users can interact with multi-modal LLMs in a way that is like using a highlighter tool on the input context in a text editor, so they can emphasize the parts they want by highlighting them.

To get this highlighting mechanism, we build a regular and unconditional input context pair with different textual embeddings in the highlighted tokens. Then we can adjust how much the model focuses on the highlighted components using classifier-free guidance on predicted token probabilities. Also, by probing cross-token attention maps, we found a robust correlation between attention scores and the semantic significance of tokens. This suggests that in the autoregressive generation process of language models, the semantic relationship between tokens can be represented to some extent by their attention scores. Based on this, we introduce an attention activation strategy that adjusts the attention weights for a highlighted part. Prompt Highlighter uses an adjusted attention mask to reweight the corresponding attention scores, so the generation focuses more on the highlighted parts.

Compared to vanilla inference, our highlighted inference can guide the generation process to produce controllable results that are closer to what users need, as illustrated in the figure. Prompt Highlighter is compatible with mainstream transformer-based multi-modal LLMs. This includes VLMs that use precise patch-wise visual token mapping, like LLaVA, and also methods that use implicit query-based visual token mapping, like the ones based on Q-Former. This new way of interacting through highlighted sections during generation goes beyond what prompt engineering can do.

We also show the effectiveness of Prompt Highlighter by evaluating it on comprehensive multi-modal benchmarks. We verify that directly highlighting the full image context in VLMs can significantly improve the quality of generated image captions and question-answering results. Our method can effectively reduce the model's tendency to hallucinate by guiding its focus toward reliable contexts, which improves the overall performance. Without additional training, our method improves the performance of the baseline LLaVA-v1.5 and gets 2nd place in both the MMBench and MME-perception leaderboards.

Our contributions are: (1) We are the first to explore fine-grained human-model interactions in multi-modal LLMs, and we propose a plug-and-play pipeline that enables token-level user interactions for controllable generation. (2) We do extensive experiments on comprehensive benchmarks and show that our method significantly improves the overall performance.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Large Language Models (LLMs) have driven significant progress in a multitude of natural language processing tasks [1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9]. Further advances have come from extending these models to vision-language tasks [10,11,12,13,14,15] through visual-language alignment and instruction tuning, leading to Vision Language Models (VLMs) that generate text based on multi-modal inputs. Due to their autoregressive nature, the typical generation process in LLMs and VLMs (multi-modal LLMs) is primarily conditioned on input contexts. Prompt engineering [16,17,18,19] has emerged as a common interaction mechanism between humans and language models, in which diverse formats and content of prompts are used to steer generation towards desired outcomes. However, prompt engineering often relies on empirical intuition and requires careful context design, making it less accessible to non-experts. As illustrated in the left part of the figure, even meticulously crafted prompts that clearly convey the concept of ‘compactness’ can lead to unpredictable outputs that fail to meet the requirements.

Instead of manipulating prompt-level contexts (i.e., prompt engineering) to control LMs’ generation, we propose a novel inference approach, Prompt Highlighter, that enables token-level user interactions for personalized generation. Our method lets users interact with multi-modal LLMs much as they would apply a highlighter tool to the input context in a text editor, emphasizing desired parts by highlighting them.

This highlighting mechanism is achieved by constructing a regular and unconditional input context pair with different textual embeddings in the highlighted tokens. We can then adjust the model’s focus on the highlighted components by applying classifier-free guidance [20,21,22] to predicted token probabilities. Moreover, by probing cross-token attention maps, we discover a robust correlation between attention scores and the semantic significance of tokens, suggesting that in the autoregressive generation process of language models, the semantic relationship between tokens can be represented to a certain extent by their attention scores. Building on this insight, we introduce an attention activation strategy that adjusts the attention weights associated with a highlighted part: Prompt Highlighter employs an adjusted attention mask to reweight the corresponding attention scores, enabling more focused generation on highlighted parts.

As illustrated in the figure, compared to vanilla inference, our highlighted inference guides the generation process to produce controllable results that align more closely with user needs. Prompt Highlighter is compatible with mainstream transformer-based multi-modal LLMs, including VLMs that use precise patch-wise visual token mapping, such as LLaVA [10,23,24], as well as methods that employ implicit query-based visual token mapping, like those based on Q-Former [13,15,14,11]. This novel paradigm of interacting through highlighted sections during generation goes beyond what prompt engineering can offer.

We further demonstrate the effectiveness of Prompt Highlighter on comprehensive multi-modal benchmarks. We verify that directly highlighting the full image context in VLMs significantly improves the quality of generated image captions [25] and question-answering results. In particular, our method effectively mitigates the model’s propensity to hallucinate by guiding its focus toward reliable contexts, which enhances overall performance. Notably, without additional training, our method improves the baseline LLaVA-v1.5, securing 2 {}^{\text{nd}} place in both the MMBench [26] and MME-perception [27] leaderboards.

Our contributions are as follows: (1) We pioneer the exploration of fine-grained human-model interactions in multi-modal LLMs, proposing a plug-and-play pipeline that enables token-level user interactions for controllable generation. (2) We conduct extensive experiments on comprehensive benchmarks, showing that our method significantly enhances overall performance.
